pr_body:
Add a new provider API to allow a provider to be set as the default entropy source for `RAND_bytes()` et al..
The provider that will be used as the entropy source can be set both programatically and via configuration on a per library context basis.  This permits libcrypto to use the FIPS providers _internal_ DRBGs directly which means that the CRNG tests of the entropy source are used.  It also provides an easier way for third party entropy source providers to be linked into libcrypto.

Fixes #24094

- [x] documentation is added or updated
- [x] tests are added or updated

@paulidale I am not sure I understand the placement of this function as a functions provided to the core.

All providers already provide operations via the query_operation functions and there already is a OSS_OP_RAND operation that provides random data.

I would expect this new function to be added there as one of the provided operations of the "OP_RAND" provider.

It does mean that ossl_provider_random() will have to use query_operations for OSSL_OP_RAND and then check for the function in that table, but this is what is done everywhere else, doesn't look particularly difficult.

> @paulidale I am not sure I understand the placement of this function as a functions provided to the core.
…
> I would expect this new function to be added there as one of the provided operations of the "OP_RAND" provider.

The hassle is getting a pointer to the DRBGs which live deep inside the FIPS provider's _internal_ lib context.  They simply are not available from the outside.  Thus we **need** a provider level function for this, rather than an algorithm level one.  Yes, the provider level function could be `EVP_RAND_fetch_internal()` which selects a specific internal object (by name since addresses aren't meaningful or available, so "primary", "public" or "private") but that path is kludgy and, quite frankly, more complex.

I'm going to draw up some diagrams to help explain this messy situation.

# The situation as the code currently stands looks like:

![PauliCAD current](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/assets/17916609/df3e7f3f-b9a3-455d-8a28-24a3dc46e648)

A user application that calls `RAND_bytes()` or friends, will draw the randomness from the public DRBG.  This is seeded from the seed-src via the primary DRBG.  The problem is that the FIPS mandated CRNG tests are not be used on the raw entropy source.

Note that the FIPS provider has it's own internal DRBG chains which does include the CRNG testing.  This means that any call to `RAND_bytes()` from insider the FIPS provider operates correctly.  By design, the entropy source the FIPS provider uses lives in libcrypto and isn't validated.  This means we get an entropy caveat on our FIPS validation but it saves us having to validate lots of platforms' operating system sources.

Also note that the DRBG's used by libcrypto are created from the FIPS provider, so their compliance isn't a concern.  This is also true for all the other options discussed below.

# What this PR does:

![PauliCAD changes](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/assets/17916609/f5ace959-56b6-47b9-af2e-e432f905135d)

A new provider API is added that allows a provider to become the randomness source for `RAND_bytes()`.  The calling application (or libcrypto) calls `RAND_bytes()` and this gets diverted to the FIPS provider if it's been loaded.  If the FIPS provider hasn't been loaded, the request is satisfied via libcrypto's DRBGs etc.

This new provider API can also be used by other RNG providers to replace the FIPS provider and libcrypto's DRBG chains.  On small devices with HW RNG, this is easier than implementing the full EVP RAND interface.

Note that libcrypto's DRBGs will _only_ be populated if the FIPS (or other randomness) provider isn't in use.  I.e. the expectation is that they wouldn't exist.

# Alternative:

![PauliCAD CRNGT as RAND](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/assets/17916609/efb012db-fb81-406d-96a0-1ebb146da357)

The possibility of creating a new EVP_RAND object that passed through entropy while applying the CRNG testing was also considered.  While it would have been workable, it would also have been:

1. more complex to implement and
2. it notably requires libcrypto to be aware of the FIPS provider being loaded or not.

Having libcrypto change its behaviour based on the providers loaded would set a poor precedent and it would make life difficult for third parties who want to write their own FIPS validated providers.

# @simo5's suggestion:

![PaulCAD simo5](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/assets/17916609/38eb5e84-cd3c-492d-9c40-8a21f802b4c9)


This adds a new random object to the FIPS provider which hooks into the internal DRBG directly.  It modifies libcrypto to try to load this object before setting up it's DRBG chains.  How this would interact with the ability to specify the RNG names would need to be investigated.

As you mention, those health tests are required by SP 800-90B, specifically on the output of the noise source. Since OpenSSL doesn't implement a noise source, these tests shouldn't be implemented here (and if they would, the CRNGT is not the appropriate test). They should be implemented by your SP 800-90B compliant entropy source (e.g jitterentropy, RDSEED,...)

~Also, what about RAND_priv_bytes?~ (edited)
Nevermind, I realized later you just made a picture of one case and it wasn't comprehensive.

What I am not sure about is why you can't use the regular operations interface to source access to the drbgs.

The FIPS provider of course would use ifdefs to always short-circuit it to obtain its own internal drbgs or blow up in the process.

I was thinking this table would be extended:
```
static const OSSL_ALGORITHM fips_rands[] = {
    { PROV_NAMES_CTR_DRBG, FIPS_DEFAULT_PROPERTIES, ossl_drbg_ctr_functions },
    { PROV_NAMES_HASH_DRBG, FIPS_DEFAULT_PROPERTIES, ossl_drbg_hash_functions },
    { PROV_NAMES_HMAC_DRBG, FIPS_DEFAULT_PROPERTIES, ossl_drbg_ossl_hmac_functions },                                
    { PROV_NAMES_TEST_RAND, FIPS_UNAPPROVED_PROPERTIES, ossl_test_rng_functions },                                   
+   { PROV_NAMES_RANDOM, FIPS_DEFAULT_PROPERTIES, ossl_provider_random },
    { NULL, NULL, NULL }                                                                                             
};                                                                                                                   
```

And this is a table that would provide access to the instantiated public and private drbg, with something like:
```
const OSSL_DISPATCH ossl_provider_random_functions[] = {
    { OSSL_FUNC_RANDOM_PUBLIC_DRBG, (void(*)(void))public_drbg_wrapper },
    { OSSL_FUNC_RANDOM_PRIVATE_DRBG, (void(*)(void))private_drbg_wrapper },
    OSSL_DISPATCH_END
};
```

RAND_bytes would call the usual mechanism to get the wrapper, and will get what the properties force. In FIPS mode the properties are normally set to fips=yes so the only provider that will be able to fulfill those will be the fips provider (of course you may have to implement some fallback if none of the providers offer this so that older fips.so providers can still be used).

The mechanism above allows to create a custom provider (call it rdrand) that offer just the random stuff (like the old RDRAND engine), and then by setting ?provider=rdrand as default EVP_properties you can get it used in preference whenever possible.

(edit) bonus points, if we keep public and private random as separate functions you could offer a random source just for the public or just the private bytes cases.

> As you mention, those health tests are required by SP 800-90B, specifically on the output of the noise source. Since OpenSSL doesn't implement a noise source, these tests shouldn't be implemented here (and if they would, the CRNGT is not the appropriate test). They should be implemented by your SP 800-90B compliant entropy source (e.g jitterentropy, RDSEED,...)

Hmmmm, that's interesting.  Our lab told us the tests had to be done on the input to the DRBGs.  It's the same location but a different viewpoint.  Might be worthwhile asking the lab again about this?

> Hmmmm, that's interesting. Our lab told us the tests had to be done on the input to the DRBGs. It's the same location but a different viewpoint. Might be worthwhile asking the lab again about this?

If no conditioning component is implemented, then it's indeed the same location. However, from a conceptual standpoint it doesn't really make sense to me that the *consumer* of the entropy (which OpenSSL is) would perform the health tests. An entropy source without health tests would never gain SP 800-90B validation. From SP 800-90B, page 24:
>6. Health tests **shall** be performed on the noise source samples before any conditioning is done. Additional health tests **may** be performed on the outputs of the conditioning function.

Now, you mentioned that 
> By design, the entropy source the FIPS provider uses lives in libcrypto and isn't validated. This means we get an entropy caveat on our FIPS validation but it saves us having to validate lots of platforms' operating system sources.

It sounds like you're using a different mechanism that doesn't rely on SP 800-90B. Probably FIPS 140-2 IG 7.14 Resolution 2b (== FIPS 140-3 IG 9.3.A Resolution 2b). In that case I don't really see why you need to worry about SP 800-90B health tests. I guess it wouldn't hurt to perform them at the input of the DRBG, but I don't think the CRNGT is the right test in FIPS 140-3.

Our lab was adamant that we needed to implement the tests on the inputs to the DRBGs.  Labs providing different interpretations is all too common and just adds to the confusion.  As for the tests being wrong 4.3 b permits alternatives and it's possible the lab was going to justify what we have under this category.

I think the best resolution would be for our lab to elucidate...

> Our lab was adamant that we needed to implement the tests on the inputs to the DRBGs. Labs providing different interpretations is all too common and just adds to the confusion. As for the tests being wrong 4.3 b permits alternatives and it's possible the lab was going to justify what we have under this category.

@paulidale @jvdsn 

It is to do with chaining. There is currently no way to combine multiple validated entropy sources together, thus if one does chaining, it becomes part of the conditioning functions and overall needs a new entropy cert and thus the CRNGT.

If however, there is no chaining and retrieved entropy from a validated entropy source is used as a seed without further chains primary->private chain, then CRNGT tests performed by the verified entropy source alone are sufficient.

For example:
- jitter entropy usage, without primary->private chainging - the CRNGT performed by jitter are sufficient
- a FIPS linux kernel (which typically also use jitter entropy), without primary->private chaining - the CRNGT performed in the kernel are sufficient
- I don't know how this is done in Windows & Mac OS X
- However if one keeps/adds chaining, then new CRNGT needs to be peformed on the output of the primary DRBG as that becomes the boundary for the entropy source

So what everyone is saying is simultaneously correct. Yes the openssl lab previously correctly advised to add CRGNGT tests in OpenSSL due to chaining of DRBGs that have become in scope for OpenSSL and hence Linux distro vendors had entropy certificates for both kernel & openssl, despite openssl using linux getrandom because of the chain.

If DRBGS for entropy are not chained, the boundary of the entropy source becomes smaller (scoped to jitter entropy, or the OS kernel), and thus CRGNGT implemented in the entropy source becomes sufficient. And also one doesn't then need to get a separate entropy certificate for openssl (as the entropy certificate on the jitter entropy or the OS kernel becomes sufficient).


As always confirm with your lab, as they always respond with specific guidance giving specific build & code.

> It is to do with chaining. There is currently no way to combine multiple validated entropy sources together, thus if one does chaining, it becomes part of the conditioning functions and overall needs a new entropy cert and thus the CRNGT.

Conditioning components themselves do not have entropy health testing on their outputs. Any statistical tests to assess the quality of the entropy are to be done on the noise source. I believe your lab is incorrect here.

From SP 800-90B Section 4.3:, bullet 6:

> 6. Health tests **shall** be performed on the noise source samples before any conditioning is done. Additional health tests **may** be performed on the outputs of the conditioning function. 

The purpose of 90B health testing is to ensure that the noise source is operating within bounds; given that the conditioning components in this context are effectively PRNGs in their own right, statistical testing on its output will say nothing about the noise-source's function.

> @xnox could you clarify which CRNGT you are referring to? FIPS 140-2 had such a test, but it was removed in FIPS 140-3. SP 800-90B added health tests on the output of the noise source but not after conditioning.

I affectionately combined the two distinct terms into one, sorry. I implied either FIPS 140-2 tests; or the SP 800-90B health tests. Which are affected by chaining of DRBG when operated under FIPS 140-2.

Note that it is not defined how to mix / combine / chain multiple SP 800-90B sources. Because I have attempted to certify mixing in SP 800-90B entropy with non-certified one to achieve compliance and that was untestable by the lab. (As in have a userspace jitter-entropy daemon inject entropy to the kernel).

> Note that it is not defined how to mix / combine / chain multiple SP 800-90B sources.

SP 800-90C, while in draft (and seems to be nearing completion based on John Kelsey's last discussion within the entropy working group), is used quite a bit in SP 800-90A. Of particular note is what is allowed to be used as a randomness source. 

Also in SP 800-90C is the concept of external conditioning (Sec 3.2) _(and rules for combining validated non-physical entropy sources (2.3))_. It doesn't seem necessary to get an entropy cert for what amounts to the use of an external conditioning function on the entropy data. 

> Because I have attempted to certify mixing in SP 800-90B entropy with non-certified one to achieve compliance and that was untestable by the lab. (As in have a userspace jitter-entropy daemon inject entropy to the kernel).

This is surprising to me, the SHA conditioning components can be tested (unless your kernel uses the older LFSR-conditioned JENT), and the non-certified entropy sources (the kernel-space jitter, etc.) in the noise pool could be treated as additional (i.e., non-contributing) noise.
I can't think of a situation in which it would be required to perform health tests on the conditioned output.
The advise we were given was explicit: the health tests needed to be performed on the incoming entropy and that they didn't need to be performed between in a chain.

> The advise we were given was explicit: the health tests needed to be performed on the incoming entropy and that they didn't need to be performed between in a chain.
> 
> 


To be clear: the _entropy source_ is responsible for its own health testing. OpenSSL does not need to perform health tests on the incoming entropy material and should instead rely on the entropy source to test itself.

> The advise we were given was explicit: the health tests needed to be performed on the incoming entropy and that they didn't need to be performed between in a chain.

can you please quote / share that advice, with supporting references?
I no longer have the emails in question.

issue_context.title: FIPS CRNG testing not correct
issue_context.body:
Report about the FIPS provider not running the CRNG testing correctly:

> We came across that the RNG initialization using syscall in 3.0 fetches
> the data (48 bytes in our case) in one syscall and in 3.2.1 it takes a
> different code patch (presumably because of #22394) and at the end fetches
> 48 bytes as one chunk that looks like breaking the FIPS requirements
> to us. Previously the seeding was through crngt and fetched 16 bytes in
> unpatched code.
> 
> The reproducer is simply openssl rand 1 in FIPS mode.

The FIPS provider is doing things correctly internally.  Thus, key generation will meet the standards.  However, generating random bytes from outside of the boundary using the FIPS providers DRBG's will skip the CRNG testing which is a violation of the standards.
comments:
@paulidale given the current FIPS certification queue, I think we should first look at solutions that don't require changes to the earliest version of the fips provider.

Ignoring all the the other requirements (for unit tests, custom entropy sources, etc.), and assuming that openssl is running on a system where if if does `getrandom(..., 32, GRND_RANDOM)`, it will get 256 bits of entropy from a FIPS compliant CRNG, can we modify libcrypto in a way that `RAND_bytes` and `RAND_priv_bytes` will be FIPS compliant?

@paulidale given that FIPS-140-3 is a full test cycle, for which making a FIPS provider-altering change shouldn't affect any queue positions, is it worth considering the above change for prior releases, making RAND_bytes and RAND_priv_bytes fips compilant in such a way that the seed source could be selected in master?

If so, what might such a change look like?

I'm pretty sure I tried the above suggestion and there were problems with it not passing tests.  Moreover:

1. it skips the RNG health tests outside of FIPS mode (so doesn't address the underlying issue); and
2. it would be a breaking change for a number of our uses because the ability to specify the seed source and DRBG rands was requested and is in use.

I really don't think what I suggested earlier is a good approach to solving this.

The approach in #24498 is better IMO and it would also let us fully remove the deprecated RAND_METHOD code.
For the 140-2 validation I see two possibilities:
1. back port the eventual fix which requires revalidation, fortunately the changes on the FIPS side would almost certainly be considered non-security critical; or
2. play three monkeys and ignore the problem.

There is a final, and by far the best, option which depends on the answer to the question to the lab.  If the health tests really aren't required inside the FIPS boundary, life is **much** easier.
